brief.situation: 22:00 in a medical ICU. You are Mrs. Olsen's nurse. She is 72, in septic shock from pneumonia, on the ordered norepinephrine through a 20-gauge peripheral IV in her left forearm while a central line is arranged. Her MAP has drifted down over 20 minutes even though the rate went up.
handover: A second working 20-gauge IV is in her right forearm, running maintenance fluid.
The hourly site check is due; the last one was at 20:55.

Unit policy for peripheral vasopressors: stop at once if extravasation is suspected, aspirate, leave the catheter for the antidote, elevate, call the intensivist, and restart the vasopressor through another working line.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What has happened at the IV site, and what do you do, in what order?

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Vasopressor extravasation: pale, cool, swollen, blanched tissue with no blood return, and a MAP that falls as the rate rises because the drug is going into the tissue.
parts.modelAnswer: The norepinephrine has extravasated: her forearm is pale, cool and swollen with no blood return, and her MAP fell even as the rate went up because the drug was going into her arm.

parts.label: In what order
parts.criteria: Stop the infusion at once; aspirate and leave the catheter for the antidote; restart the vasopressor through another working line so the MAP holds; elevate; call the intensivist for phentolamine; never flush or turn the rate up into the infiltrated site.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop it immediately, aspirate, and leave the catheter in for the phentolamine. Restart the norepinephrine in the right arm right away so her pressure holds. Elevate the arm and call the intensivist now. Don't flush it or turn it up.

expertPath.text: Site check: pale, cool, swollen, blanched, no blood return. Stop the norepinephrine there.
Aspirate and leave the catheter; restart through the right forearm IV.
Call the intensivist for phentolamine; elevate, compress, mark the border.
Assist the phentolamine infiltration; document; hourly checks.

collapse.headline: Collapse
collapse.body: Stopping an infiltrated vasopressor is right, but a patient in shock needs it restarted through another working line within minutes.

necrosis.headline: Tissue necrosis
necrosis.body: A vasopressor in the tissue causes ischemia. Stop it at once, aspirate, leave the catheter for the antidote, and never flush or turn it up into the site.

saved.headline: Arm and pressure saved
saved.body: You stopped it at once, aspirated, kept the catheter for the antidote, restarted through the other arm and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

savedGaps.headline: Saved, with gaps
savedGaps.body: Check how fast you stopped and called, whether the catheter stayed in for the antidote, and whether more drug went in.

time_up.headline: Untreated
time_up.body: An extravasated vasopressor needs the antidote as soon as possible.

scoring.modelReasoning: A pale, cool, swollen, blanched forearm with no blood return, and a MAP that fell as the rate rose, is norepinephrine extravasation: the drug is constricting the tissue instead of reaching her circulation. Stop the infusion immediately, aspirate what you can and leave the catheter in so the antidote can go through it, and restart the vasopressor through the other working line straight away, because she is in shock. Elevate the arm, mark the border, and call the intensivist for phentolamine infiltrated as soon as possible, as the label directs. Never flush the line or turn the rate up into the infiltrated site.
